finding: The corrected-engine repeats confirm that first order and MUSCL-off/RK2 recover the secondary slowdown and depth rise at G2 much better on the coarse mesh. The controlled ablations identify velocity reconstruction as the stronger sensitivity: retaining surface/depth reconstruction but removing velocity slopes gives G2 level/speed RMSE of 0.02337 m and 0.2565 m/s; retaining velocity reconstruction alone gives 0.05394 m and 0.8069 m/s. Shared velocity limiting passes the native accuracy checks and produces a brief slowdown around 20–22 s, but flow accelerates again by 23–24 s. Its speed RMSE is 0.7286 m/s and it does not sustain the observed depth rise. These results localize a numerical sensitivity; they do not prove that the extra first-order diffusion is physically correct.
qualification: All five configurations pass all 16 analytical cases (80 passes). The baseline and shared-velocity candidate pass all 12 native checks. Coupling all four limiter factors fails the affine-field accuracy test and is excluded from Test 6. The surface/depth-only ablation passes 10/12 native checks and the velocity-only ablation 9/12: their recorded failures require the reconstructed slopes intentionally removed by the ablations. Both pass the remaining safety/consistency checks and all analytical cases, and are admitted solely as diagnostic controls. They are not qualified production second-order alternatives. All 24 baseline CPU regression tests pass. The short replay matches time, depth and both velocity components bit for bit.
accuracy: On the coarse mesh, first order and MUSCL-off/RK2 improve all five available measured quantity/gauge errors relative to the corrected order-2 control. Refinement remains mixed: MUSCL-off G2 level RMSE increases from 0.01347 to 0.03496 m while speed RMSE decreases from 0.2860 to 0.2389 m/s. The broad-mesh MUSCL-off G4 speed RMSE is 0.2692 m/s versus 0.2237 m/s for broad-mesh order 2. The shared-velocity candidate worsens G2 level RMSE from 0.05552 to 0.05759 m and G4 speed from 0.2575 to 0.2832 m/s, while improving G5 level. There is no demonstrated convergence to the recovered measurements or uniformly better second-order replacement.
front: At 20 s, the fitted coarse-mesh front is at x=2.862 m with corrected order 2, x=2.392 m with first order, and x=2.396 m with MUSCL-off/RK2; G2 is at x=2.650 m. Removing velocity slopes while retaining scalar reconstruction puts it at x=2.359 m, with G2 depth 0.11125 m and speed 0.4365 m/s. Removing scalar slopes while retaining velocity reconstruction leaves the front at x=2.856 m, with G2 depth 0.02926 m and speed 1.6412 m/s. Thus the recovered G2 response accompanies a substantial front displacement. The first-order broad mesh moves the fitted front to x=2.536 m, showing residual spatial sensitivity. These are computed front positions, not an independently measured spatial jump map. With shared velocity limiting, the fitted front moves from x=2.741 m at 18 s to x=2.617 m at 21 s and back to x=2.700 m at 24 s. G2 depth/speed changes from 0.0652 m / 0.8823 m/s at 21 s to 0.0260 m / 1.6584 m/s at 24 s. Its partial improvement is therefore transient; the fitted front is not a sharp boundary between uniform states.
decision: Continue development around velocity reconstruction and limiting, using independently specified oblique/reflected hydraulic jumps and rotation-equivalence tests to assess a multidimensional or characteristic limiter and any general shock sensor. Preserve admissible smooth linear fields, still-water balance, positivity, conservation and bank-release stability before returning to every available Test 6 gauge and a declared mesh sequence. Existing first order remains useful as a labelled sensitivity. A shared velocity limiter alone is insufficient, and the slope-removal ablations deliberately sacrifice formal accuracy. No experimental control is promoted to a production option or a new default.
